1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune pretrained language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual observations and language instructions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}, but which of the resulting representational changes reflect action training and which are inherited from the pretrained backbone?
5	In these decoder-only architectures, image tokens precede instruction tokens, and the causal attention mask restricts multimodal integration to a single readout token~\cite{wang2025seeing,pei2025rethinking}; how representations at this critical position are reshaped by action fine-tuning remains unknown.
6	
7	Behavioral studies show that VLAs exhibit visual dominance~\cite{grant2026} and underweight instructions~\cite{haon2025}, but existing representational analyses target single architectures.
8	No prior work tests whether instruction routing---the internal mechanisms by which instruction tokens influence action-relevant representations---is consistent across backbone families or decomposes training-associated effects from inherited base-model priors.
9	
10	We address this gap with a cross-architecture analysis of three VLAs (OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla}, TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla}, and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora}) across four LIBERO~\cite{liu2023_libero} task suites (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
11	TraceVLA and NORA baselines are pure VLMs ($N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions); OpenVLA's baseline is the OXE-pretrained~\cite{padalkar2023_oxe} VLA (VLA-to-VLA transition).
12	
13	\begin{figure}[t]
14	\centering
15	\includegraphics[width=0.88\linewidth]{figures/fig_overview.pdf}
16	\caption{\textbf{Analysis framework.} We analyze hidden states at image-token averages and the readout token via layer-wise action probes, counterfactual instruction perturbations, and L1 attention profiling to distinguish training-associated changes from inherited backbone priors.}
17	\label{fig:overview}
18	\end{figure}
19	
20	Our analysis reveals three findings (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): (1)~VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning is associated with substantial $R^2$ exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.16$--$0.46$), whereas VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning and reference models show only small fluctuations ($\Delta R^2 < 0.10$), with three NLP controls (all $\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) confirming transition-type specificity; (2)~all trained VLAs exhibit medium-to-large counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$); and (3)~L1 instruction attention reflects base-model priors, not VLA training (\S\ref{sec:r2_collapse}--\ref{sec:l1_priors}).
21	While concurrent work evaluates VLA instruction-following behaviorally~\cite{fang2026when,swann2026}, we provide complementary representational analysis of how instruction information is routed internally.
22	
23	\noindent\textbf{Our contributions:}
24	\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
25	\item A cross-architecture representational analysis of three VLAs, combining trained/reference controls with token-level probing across a $3 \times 4$ architecture-suite matrix.
26	\item Evidence that $R^2$ exit collapse is associated with VLM-to-VLA transitions ($\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ across two architectures) but not with VLA-to-VLA fine-tuning or NLP instruction tuning of the same backbones.
27	\item A decomposition of VLA instruction routing into training-associated effects and inherited base-model priors, based on cross-architecture trained/reference contrasts.
28	\end{enumerate}
29

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

We investigate how action-relevant representations are organized across three VLA architectures using complementary probing, attention, and perturbation analyses.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Architectures and Data}
\label{sec:arch_data}

\looseness=-1
We study three VLAs spanning distinct backbone families (Table~\ref{tab:arch_overview}):
\textbf{OpenVLA}~\cite{kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024} (Llama-2-7B~\cite{touvron2023_llama2}, 32 layers, pretrained on Open X-Embodiment~\cite{padalkar2023_oxe} [OXE; 970K episodes]),
\textbf{TraceVLA}~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} (Phi-3-mini~\cite{abdin2024phi3}, 32 layers, trained on an OXE subset with spatial trace conditioning), and
\textbf{NORA}~\cite{hung2025nora} (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, 36 layers, grouped-query attention with 16 query heads).
Each is evaluated in trained and reference conditions.
A critical asymmetry distinguishes the references: OpenVLA's is an OXE-pretrained VLA (already producing actions), while TraceVLA and NORA references are pure VLMs (Phi-3-Vision, Qwen2.5-VL) with no action training; thus OpenVLA comparisons measure VLA-to-VLA transitions, while TraceVLA and NORA measure VLM-to-VLA transitions.
OpenVLA additionally provides Llama-2 base and random-weight conditions (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).

We evaluate on LIBERO~\cite{liu2023_libero}, comprising four task suites (Goal, Spatial, Object, Long-Horizon) with 10 tasks and 50 demonstrations each.
The three architectures and four suites form a $3 \times 4$ matrix; 10 of 12 cells are filled (NORA Object and Long-Horizon lack available checkpoints).

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Representation Extraction}
\looseness=-1
From each architecture, we extract hidden states at every transformer layer from two token positions: (a)~\textbf{image\_mean}, the mean activation over image tokens, and (b)~\textbf{readout}, the hidden state at the final pre-action token, which can attend to all preceding context.
L0 denotes the embedding layer, L1--L$N$ the post-transformer hidden states ($N = 32$ for OpenVLA/TraceVLA, $36$ for NORA).
We cross training status (trained vs.\ reference) $\times$ instruction presence (with vs.\ without) across all 10 cells.
OpenVLA additionally provides DinoSigLIP projector, DINOv2, and CLIP representations for the single-architecture analyses (\S\ref{sec:openvla_routing}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_rsa_perlayer_curve.pdf}
\caption{Per-layer RSA ($\rho$) for trained/reference OpenVLA. Trained: inverted-U peaking at L12; reference: monotonic decline. Readout and image\_mean diverge after L12.}
\label{fig:rsa_perlayer}
\end{figure}

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-Architecture Analyses}
\label{sec:cross_arch_analyses}

Three analyses are applied to every available cell in the $3 \times 4$ matrix.

\paragraph{Action probes.}\looseness=-1
Two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} predict 7-DoF actions from frozen representations (details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
Probe $R^2$ measures decodability, not causal usage.
$\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$; we use $> 0.10$ as the threshold for substantial peak-to-exit reduction.
Demo-level train/test splits and Monte Carlo cross-validation ($n = 1{,}000$) provide 95\% CIs (Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}); linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe}).

\paragraph{L1 attention head profiling.}\looseness=-1
To determine whether attention heads preferentially route instruction information to the readout position, each L1 head is classified as instruction-dominant ($>50\%$ of readout-token attention to instruction tokens) or image-dominant, reported as $k/N$ heads (32 for MHA, 16 for GQA).
Sensitivity analysis at thresholds from $30\%$ to $70\%$ confirms ordering robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold_sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Counterfactual instruction perturbation.}\looseness=-1
To test whether the model's actions depend on instruction content, the instruction is replaced with four conditions: empty string, wrong task, shuffled tokens, and paraphrased.
We measure trained-model sensitivity via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TraceVLA) or cosine distance (NORA); reference VLMs use cosine distance on hidden representations.
These metrics operate on different scales; cross-metric ratios are invalid (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).

\looseness=-1
OpenVLA additionally supports cross-instruction probes, representational similarity analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, and external baselines (DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2}, CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip}); these single-architecture methods are detailed in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}.
Figure~\ref{fig:rsa_perlayer} previews this: per-layer geometric alignment ($\rho$) diverges between trained and reference models after L12, with trained readout tokens maintaining alignment ($\rho = 0.584$) while image-mean representations decay ($\rho = 0.422$), suggesting task-specific conditioning at the readout position.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_matrix_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Cross-architecture analysis matrix.} Three architectures (OpenVLA, TraceVLA, NORA) $\times$ four LIBERO suites; 10 of 12 cells filled. Color encodes $\Delta R^2$ (peak$-$exit); bold borders mark VLM-to-VLA transitions exhibiting substantial exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 > 0.10$).}
\label{fig:result_matrix}
\end{figure}

\FloatBarrier

2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	\looseness=-1
5	We presented a cross-architecture representational analysis of instruction routing in vision-language-action models, studying three VLAs built on distinct backbone families across four LIBERO task suites.
6	Our three complementary analyses---layer-wise action probing, counterfactual instruction perturbation, and L1 attention profiling---consistently decompose VLA instruction routing into two distinct patterns: training-associated effects and inherited base-model priors.
7	Exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.16$--$0.46$) and graded counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$) emerge specifically from VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning---absent in both VLA-to-VLA and NLP-only controls---while L1 attention routing is inherited from reference backbones.
8	These findings enable practical diagnostics: $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ flags under-utilized exit-layer representations without rollouts, and mid-layer features offer principled tap points for downstream reward models and planners.
9	The cross-architecture consistency---with mid-layer action-probe peaks converging to within $R^2 = 0.003$ despite divergent reference profiles---suggests these are general properties of autoregressive VLA fine-tuning, not artifacts of any single model design.
10	
11	\section{Limitations}
12	\label{sec:limitations}
13	
14	\looseness=-1
15	Our conclusions rest on $N{=}2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions plus one VLA-to-VLA case, all autoregressive decoders evaluated on a single benchmark (LIBERO); flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} action heads may behave differently.
16	All findings are correlational---$R^2$ measures decodability, not causal reliance---and evaluations are open-loop; the $\Delta R^2$--success-rate correlation ($\rho{=}0.583$, $p{=}0.10$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}) is suggestive but underpowered ($n{=}9$).
17	Extending to additional architectures, non-autoregressive action heads, and closed-loop behavioral validation are priorities for future work.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

\looseness=-1
We presented a cross-architecture representational analysis of instruction routing in vision-language-action models, studying three VLAs built on distinct backbone families across four LIBERO task suites.
Our three complementary analyses---layer-wise action probing, counterfactual instruction perturbation, and L1 attention profiling---consistently decompose VLA instruction routing into two distinct patterns: training-associated effects and inherited base-model priors.
Exit collapse ($\Delta R^2 = 0.16$--$0.46$) and graded counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$) emerge specifically from VLM-to-VLA fine-tuning---absent in both VLA-to-VLA and NLP-only controls---while L1 attention routing is inherited from reference backbones.
These findings enable practical diagnostics: $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ flags under-utilized exit-layer representations without rollouts, and mid-layer features offer principled tap points for downstream reward models and planners.
The cross-architecture consistency---with mid-layer action-probe peaks converging to within $R^2 = 0.003$ despite divergent reference profiles---suggests these are general properties of autoregressive VLA fine-tuning, not artifacts of any single model design.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\looseness=-1
Our conclusions rest on $N{=}2$ VLM-to-VLA transitions plus one VLA-to-VLA case, all autoregressive decoders evaluated on a single benchmark (LIBERO); flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} action heads may behave differently.
All findings are correlational---$R^2$ measures decodability, not causal reliance---and evaluations are open-loop; the $\Delta R^2$--success-rate correlation ($\rho{=}0.583$, $p{=}0.10$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}) is suggestive but underpowered ($n{=}9$).
Extending to additional architectures, non-autoregressive action heads, and closed-loop behavioral validation are priorities for future work.

    ('NORA', 'Goal'): 0.455,
    ('NORA', 'Spatial'): 0.308,
    ('NORA', 'Object'): None,
    ('NORA', 'Long'): None,
}

THRESHOLD = 0.10
nrows = len(architectures)
ncols = len(suites)

cell_h = 0.78

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""fig_claim_evidence: Claim-evidence-scope summary figure (Appendix)."""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'serif',
    'font.serif': ['Liberation Serif'],
    'pdf.fonttype': 42,
    'ps.fonttype': 42,
    'mathtext.fontset': 'custom',
    'mathtext.rm': 'Liberation Serif',
    'mathtext.it': 'Liberation Serif:italic',
    'mathtext.bf': 'Liberation Serif:bold',
})
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
import os

rows = [
    {
        'finding': 'Training-Associated\nExit Collapse',
        'description': '$R^2$ drops at exit layers\nafter VLA fine-tuning',
        'evidence': '6/6 VLM→VLA conditions\nshow Δ > 0.10;\n0/4 VLA→VLA;\n0/10 reference conditions',
        'limitation': 'Correlational,\nnot causal',
        'color': '#FDEBD0',
        'edge': '#E8A838',
    },
    {
        'finding': 'Action-Relevant\nSensitivity',
        'description': 'Counterfactual perturbation\nreveals action-linked\nrepresentations',
        'evidence': "Cohen's $d$ ≥ 0.45 across\n8 trained conditions;\nempty ranks first in 6/8",
        'limitation': '$d$ vs cosine metric\nincomparability',
        'color': '#D5F5E3',
        'edge': '#52BE80',
    },
    {
        'finding': 'Inherited Instruction\nAttention Prior',
        'description': 'L1 attention patterns\ninherited from\npre-trained VLMs',
        'evidence': 'Reference VLMs already\nshow task-structured\nattention',
        'limitation': 'Not causally\ntested',
        'color': '#D6EAF8',
        'edge': '#5DADE2',
    },
]

col_labels = ['Finding', 'Evidence', 'Limitation']
col_colors = ['#2C3E50', '#2C3E50', '#2C3E50']

fig_w, fig_h = 7.0, 3.2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(fig_w, fig_h))
ax.set_xlim(0, fig_w)
ax.set_ylim(0, fig_h)
ax.axis('off')

box_h = 0.72
row_gap = 0.18
top_y = fig_h - 0.55

col_x = [0.15, 1.65, 3.35, 5.55]
col_w = [1.35, 1.55, 2.05, 1.25]

header_y = top_y + 0.10
header_labels = ['Finding', '', 'Evidence', 'Limitation']
for ci in [0, 2, 3]:
    cx = col_x[ci] + col_w[ci] / 2
    ax.text(cx, header_y, header_labels[ci], ha='center', va='bottom',
            fontsize=11, fontweight='bold', color='#2C3E50')

for ri, row in enumerate(rows):
    y_center = top_y - ri * (box_h + row_gap) - box_h / 2

    for ci, (key, x, w) in enumerate(zip(
        ['finding', 'description', 'evidence', 'limitation'],
        col_x, col_w
    )):
        if ci == 0:
            fc = row['color']
            ec = row['edge']
            fw = 'bold'
            fs = 9
        elif ci == 1:
            fc = '#FAFAFA'
            ec = '#CCCCCC'
            fw = 'normal'
            fs = 8
        elif ci == 2:
            fc = '#F0F7FC'
            ec = '#85C1E9'
            fw = 'normal'
            fs = 8
        else:
            fc = '#FDF2F2'
            ec = '#E6A0A0'
            fw = 'normal'
            fs = 8

        rect = mpatches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (x, y_center - box_h / 2), w, box_h,
            boxstyle='round,pad=0.06',
            facecolor=fc, edgecolor=ec, linewidth=1.2
        )
        ax.add_patch(rect)
        ax.text(x + w / 2, y_center, row[key],
                ha='center', va='center', fontsize=fs, fontweight=fw,
                color='#333333', linespacing=1.3)

    for ci in range(3):
        x_start = col_x[ci] + col_w[ci] + 0.02
        x_end = col_x[ci + 1] - 0.02
        ax.annotate('', xy=(x_end, y_center), xytext=(x_start, y_center),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#888888',
                                     lw=1.5, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))

plt.tight_layout(pad=0.2)

_REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
out_dirs = [
    os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'docs', 'paper', 'figures'),
    os.path.join(_REPO_ROOT, 'artifacts', 'figures', 'paper'),
]
for d in out_dirs:
    os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, 'fig_claim_evidence.pdf'), dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(d, 'fig_claim_evidence.png'), dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')

plt.close()
print('Saved fig_claim_evidence.')
